text: There are n gas stations arranged in a circle. At station i you get gas of i. Driving from station i to the next station costs cost of i. You start with an empty tank. Return the index of the station where you can start and drive the full loop clockwise. If there is no such station, return negative one.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — at each station I first add the gas there, then pay the cost to reach the next one. The tank can hit exactly zero, but it can never go below zero. And a full loop means I come back to where I started. Is that right?
Yes. And if an answer exists, it's unique.

Good, that helps. Then the only number that really matters at each station is the net change — I'll call it diff, which is the gas at that station minus the cost to leave it. The tank after any stretch of road is just the sum of the diffs on that stretch. So I can think of the whole thing as a circle of numbers, and I need a starting point where the running sum never goes negative. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and ten to the fifth, and every gas and cost value is between zero and ten to the fourth.

Got it. Up to a hundred thousand stations, so I want linear time. Let me run through the example. Gas is one, two, three, four, five, and cost is three, four, five, one, two. So the diffs are minus two, minus two, minus two, three, three. If I start at station three, my tank goes three, then six, then four, then two, then zero. I make it back with an empty tank, so the answer is three. That matches. The second example: gas is two, three, four, and cost is three, four, three. The diffs are minus one, minus one, and one, and they add up to minus one. The whole loop burns more gas than it gives, so no start can work, and the answer is negative one. That also matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to try every start, and drive the loop from it until the tank goes negative. That's quadratic. With a hundred thousand stations, that's up to ten to the tenth steps — way too slow. Another quick idea is to start at the station with the biggest diff. But that's wrong. Take gas zero, one, two, and cost three, zero, zero. The biggest diff is at station two, but the real answer is station one. Starting from one, I save up one plus two, which is three — just enough for the three I need at station zero. This problem reminds me of a greedy with a running sum, like Kadane's algorithm: keep a sum, and when it goes negative, throw it away and start fresh. The real question is why throwing it away is safe here. The key fact is a skip lemma. Say I start at s, and the tank first goes negative at i. Then no station from s through i can be the start. Let me walk through that. Pick any station k in between. When I drove from s, I reached k with some tank that was at least zero. If I start at k instead, I reach it with exactly zero. So I'm never better off. I'd have at most the same gas all the way to i — and I already failed there. So I can jump the start straight to i plus one, and every station gets looked at just once.
Okay. But after one pass, how do you know the last start you picked really works?

That's the second fact: an answer exists exactly when the total of all the diffs is at least zero. If the total is negative, the loop costs more than it gives, so nothing works. If the total is at least zero, the last candidate start works. Here's why. From start to the end of the array, the running sum never went negative — that's how start survived. Then I wrap around to station zero and drive the part before start. That part is made of pieces that each failed, so each one has a negative sum. But inside a piece, the sum only dips below zero at its very end. So the lowest my tank can ever get is at the very end of the loop, and at that point it holds exactly the total, which is at least zero. In other words, the part before start is paid for by the total being non-negative. So there are really two separate jobs. The total answers: is there an answer at all? And the current tank, together with start, answers: which station is it?

Here's the plan. I keep three integers: total, cur, and start, all beginning at zero. Total is the sum of every diff, and it tells me whether an answer exists. Cur is the tank since the current candidate start, and it tells me which station. I loop over every station once. At each one I compute the diff, and add it to both total and cur. If cur drops below zero, then nothing from start through i works, so I move start to i plus one, and reset cur to zero. At the end, if total is negative I return negative one, otherwise I return start. Total is never reset — it always covers the whole loop. One thing worth flagging — the two comparisons are both strict, and both on purpose. Cur less than zero, not less than or equal: an empty tank is still fine, I just can't go below zero. And total less than zero, not less than or equal: a total of exactly zero is a valid loop. I come back with an empty tank, just like in example one. There's a trade-off here. I could do two passes — first sum everything to check the total, then a second pass to find the start. That's a bit easier to read. But both jobs only need the same diffs, so one pass does both, with just three integers. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up, and I'll talk through it rather than read it out. I grab n from the size of the gas array, and set total, cur, and start to zero. Then a single for loop over i. Inside, diff is gas of i minus cost of i, and I add it to total and to cur. If cur is below zero, start becomes i plus one and cur goes back to zero. After the loop, I return negative one if total is below zero, and start otherwise. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — start equals i plus one can end up equal to n, which is out of range. But that only happens if the very last station fails. Then every piece of the array went negative, so the total is negative, and I return negative one instead. Whenever the total is at least zero, start is never n — in my tests that happened zero times. I also checked what breaks if I get a small detail wrong. I tested every input with n from one to five and values from zero to three, keeping the six hundred twelve thousand, two hundred forty inputs that meet the unique-answer rule. Setting start to i instead of i plus one: ninety-one thousand, nine hundred twenty-two wrong. The smallest is gas zero, one with cost one, zero — it returns zero, but the answer is one. Forgetting to reset cur to zero: twenty-four thousand, six hundred ninety-nine wrong. Returning start with no total check: four hundred ninety-six thousand, seven hundred twenty-eight wrong — that's every single negative-one case. Writing total less than or equal to zero: seventy-one thousand and ninety-two wrong, and it fails exactly when the tank ends empty. Writing cur less than or equal to zero: fourteen thousand, five hundred eleven wrong — gas zero, cost zero returns one, which isn't even a valid index. And starting at the station with the largest diff: twenty-seven thousand, one hundred seventy-nine wrong. So every piece of this short code is doing real work.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one: gas one through five, cost three, four, five, one, two. Expected three. The first three stations each have a diff of minus two. Each time, cur drops to minus two right away, so I reset — start moves to one, then two, then three. Those rows are the skip lemma at work: each start fails immediately, so I jump past it. Now the key row, i equals three. Look at the two counters side by side. Total is still minus three, but cur is three. They tell different stories, because they do different jobs. Cur says start three is alive so far. Total says we don't know yet whether any answer exists. From here cur never goes negative — it ends at six — so start stays at three. At the end, total is exactly zero. That's the case where the strict comparison matters: with less-than-or-equal I'd wrongly return negative one here. Instead I return three. Let's also test with corner cases. Example two: total ends at minus one, so I return negative one. Correct. One station, gas zero and cost one: cur goes to minus one, start becomes one, but total is minus one, so I return negative one — the out-of-range start is never returned. One station, gas zero and cost zero: cur stays zero, no reset, total is zero, so I return zero. That single input catches both less-than-or-equal bugs. And gas zero, one with cost one, zero: reset at zero, start becomes one, total is zero, return one. Correct. Then I checked it against brute force, which tries every start and simulates. All one million, one hundred eighteen thousand, four hundred eighty inputs with n from one to five and values zero to three. On the six hundred twelve thousand, two hundred forty that meet the guarantee, there were zero mismatches. On the other five hundred six thousand, two hundred forty, which have several valid starts, the code always returned one of them. Plus twenty thousand random inputs with n up to three hundred and values up to ten to the fourth — zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. There's one loop over the stations. The start jumps forward, but it never moves back, and I never restart the loop. So each station is visited once. The time complexity is linear. The space complexity is constant: just total, cur, and start. In the worst-case scenario, the start resets at almost every station, like in example one. That's still constant work per station. The skip lemma is what lets me never look back. Oh, one more thing — overflow. Total sums up to ten to the fifth diffs, each between minus ten to the fourth and ten to the fourth. So the absolute value of total is at most ten to the ninth, which is below the maximum int. A plain int is safe here. If the limits were bigger, I'd switch to long long.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You proved the skip lemma: if the tank fails at i, nothing from start through i can work, so one pass is enough. You split the two jobs: a non-negative total says an answer exists, and you explained why the last start is that answer. And you defended both strict comparisons with one tiny input — gas zero, cost zero — where the tank ends empty. Good work.
